newsitem.title: USA: OKlahoma bomb jury on day two of deliberations.
newsitem.headline: OKlahoma bomb jury on day two of deliberations.

text.p: Jurors weighing whether convicted Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh should be put to death deliberated for a second day on Friday, while several hundred people demonstrated against the death penalty outside the courthouse.
The jury of seven men and five women began deliberating on Thursday after hearing impassioned pleas from prosecutors to vote for the death penalty and from defence lawyers to spare McVeigh's life.
McVeigh, 29, was found guilty on June 2 of murder and conspiracy charges for the April 19, 1995, bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah federal building, which killed 168 people.

At mid-morning, the jury notified lawyers and the judge that it had a question, leading to a brief, closed-door meeting. McVeigh's chief attorney Stephen Jones said afterward the question was "routine" but he did not provide details.
"Jurors have questions and the judge calls us over so that we can be informed about the question and the answer that he proposes to give them," Jones told reporters.
"They are obviously giving it careful study and proceeding in a deliberate manner," Jones said of the jury.
One of McVeigh's attorneys, Mandy Welch, met with the Gulf War veteran on Friday.

About 300 people held an anti-death penalty rally across the street from the federal courthouse. They then marched down the middle of the street in front of the courthouse. The group had a permit and police held up noon-hour traffic for the march.

"We are here to acknowledge the fact that even Timothy McVeigh as a human being has basic fundamental rights which no one, no one, has a right to violate," said David Lane, of Colorado Lawyers for Justice.

Jim Sunderland, a Jesuit priest and president of the Colorado Coalition to Abolish the Death Penalty, expressed sorrow for the victims of the bombing but said the death penalty for McVeigh would "just continue the cycle of violence that he was very much involved in."
The rally had been planned earlier, but took on additional significance because the McVeigh jury was deliberating.
McVeigh's parents and sister were in the courtroom on Thursday when Jones told the jury that if they spare McVeigh's life he may some day tell the whole story of the bombing.

"Dead men don't tell tales," Jones told the jury. "The government may not be the only people who want my client executed," he said, implying there could be others involved who would be glad to see McVeigh take his secret to the grave.
But prosecutors argued that McVeigh was a coward and a traitor and the jury should not be afraid to vote for the death penalty.

Marsha Kight, whose 23-year-old daughter, Frankie Merrell, died in the bombing, said waiting to hear McVeigh's punishment was less stressful than waiting for the guilty verdict. "What was important for me was to see him convicted. I still have an interest in this, but the big wait is over," Kight said.

She expressed empathy for McVeigh's father, Bill, saying the wait for him reminded her of what she went through waiting for word about her daughter after the bombing. Kight has said she does not believe McVeigh should be put to death.
There are only 13 people on death row in the United States for federal crimes, compared with about 3,200 who have been sentenced to die by 34 state courts.

The jury has not been sequestered during its penalty deliberations, unlike the period before it reached its guilty verdict. Lawyers for McVeigh's alleged co-conspirator Terry Nichols asked the judge to caution the jurors about any remarks they may make about Nichols, whose trial will begin later this year.

"McVeigh jurors will likely be asked by the press to speculate about Mr. Nichols' alleged involvement and the probable outcome in his upcoming trial," Nichols' attorneys wrote in their motion filed with the court.

Nichols' attorneys asked the judge to read a short statement cautioning the jurors that any remarks about Nichols "could have the effect of making it more difficult for Mr. Nichols to select an impartial jury or obtain a fair trial."
